title: Leave the Files Where They Work
description: I am making VALESKA a working index without moving the files: scan in place, classify by process, search by meaning, and let an assistant ask the catalog instead of becoming one.
body:
A knowledge-management project that starts by moving the files has already chosen the wrong work. The originals are where the work happens. Permissions live with them. Habits live with them. If you relocate the library to make the catalog easier, you have not organized knowledge. You have interrupted the value stream that produced it.

That is the problem I am solving today. VALESKA is no longer only a design document. I am building a working index around files we do not move: a scanner, an APQC classifier, PostgreSQL with pgvector, search you can call by meaning as well as by name, and a Model Context Protocol server so an assistant can use those capabilities without becoming the store.

The wrong default

Enterprise content programs still treat go-live as a migration. Folders are copied. Trees are redrawn. People are trained on a new place to put things. The old place remains, because the work never left it. You now have two memories, and neither of them describes the process.

The other default is newer and worse. Put the documents into a chat. The assistant becomes the filing cabinet. When the conversation ends, the memory ends. The access rules that belonged to the file never made the trip.

A card catalog does not require you to move the books. A process taxonomy should not require you to abandon the systems where records already live. Most people browse. They follow the road signs of work they already know. Search is the exception. If the only way to find a document is to have already moved it, the system is organizing itself, not the work.

Index rather than rearrange

I am leaving source files where they are and building a knowledge layer around them. The scanner discovers. It does not take ownership. Metadata extraction gives each record an identity: path, owner, time, type. Classification attaches the record to APQC — a shared process vocabulary — instead of a private folder dialect. Rules on paths, file types, and names are enough to start. Semantic methods can come later. They are not a substitute for a classification a person can review.

PostgreSQL holds the durable record. pgvector holds embeddings so a question can find a document by meaning, not only by filename or keyword. Hybrid search is the practical combination: exact structure plus similarity. A useful result is still a document connected to its source, its location, and the access rules that already belong to it.

The assistant is a user of that index, not the index. The command line is for direct work. FastAPI exposes the same functions to an application. The MCP server registers five tools: search, classify, scan, list categories, and retrieve file information. The assistant can ask. The platform keeps the record.

What the tests actually show

Phase 1 proved the core can run: data models, APQC classification, database connectivity, and a self-integration in which VALESKA classifies its own repository. Four tests pass.

Today I add the scanner, semantic, keyword, and hybrid search, file indexing, MCP tool registration, and integration tests. Five tests pass: MCP server, search engine, scanner, MCP tools, and their integration. Docker, environment-based configuration, and asynchronous processing are in the codebase so this is not a one-off notebook.

That is testable behavior on this repository. It is not yet proof against a real collection, a real permission model, or a real assistant in daily use. The self-integration is a necessary first patient. It is not the enterprise.

The question that remains

The architecture question from August is no longer whether a process taxonomy can be written down. It is whether an index that leaves files in place can be used — by a person and by an assistant — without becoming a second source of truth.

Can classification stay reviewable when the collection is not our own? Can retrieval keep the permission model that already exists on the file? Until those tests are run on work we did not write, this is a platform we can execute, not a claim that the collective already thinks in process.

Historical basis: VALESKA Phase 2 MCP milestone commit 8ff0b91, November 29, 2025; contemporaneous software design document, implementation plan, README, and Phase 1 and Phase 2 implementation summaries. The Phase 2 summary contains an inconsistent internal month heading; the repository commit timestamp is used as the publication-date authority.
